title: Damru symbol in jewellery: meaning and story
description: The damru is Lord Shiva's small hourglass drum. Learn the stories behind it, what its shape is said to mean, and how the motif is used in jewellery.
intro: The damru is the small, hourglass-shaped drum held by Lord Shiva, and in jewellery it usually appears as a tiny charm hanging from a trishul or as a pendant on its own. Traditionally it stands for sound, rhythm and the start of creation. If you have seen the motif and wondered why it is there, here is the story behind it and how to wear it well.

sections.heading: What the damru actually is
paragraphs: A damru is a two-headed drum shaped like an hourglass, narrow in the middle and wide at both ends. Two small beads or knots are tied to a string around the waist of the drum. When you twist the drum quickly back and forth in your wrist, the beads strike both faces and produce its familiar rattling beat. Smaller versions are still played by folk performers in many parts of India, and larger ones are used in some temple rituals and by wandering sadhus.

In images of Shiva, the damru is usually held in one hand or tied to the shaft of his trishul. As the dancing Nataraja, he holds it in his upper right hand while the other hands show fire, a gesture of protection and the raised foot.

sections.heading: The story most people know
paragraphs: The best-known tale connects the damru to the Sanskrit language itself. According to tradition, at the end of Shiva's cosmic dance he beat his damru fourteen times, and the sounds that came out were heard by the sage Panini as the fourteen Maheshwara Sutras, the sound groups that form the basis of Sanskrit grammar. Whether you take this literally or as a beautiful way of honouring the link between sound and knowledge, it explains why the damru is so closely tied to learning and music.

A broader belief, found in many devotional retellings, is that the universe began with sound, and that the damru's beat represents that first rhythm. Since Shiva is also the one who dissolves the universe in his tandava, the drum is seen as marking both beginnings and endings.

sections.heading: What the hourglass shape is said to mean
paragraphs: The damru's shape is often read as two triangles meeting at their points. One common explanation is that the two halves stand for Shiva and Shakti, or for the unmanifest and the manifest world, joining at the narrow centre where creation happens. Others see it as the rhythm of time itself, with sound moving from one side to the other.

These are interpretations rather than fixed doctrine, and you may hear different versions from different teachers. What they share is the idea that the damru is about movement and sound, which balances the stillness of Shiva in meditation.

sections.heading: Where you will see it in jewellery
paragraphs: In Indian devotional jewellery the damru turns up in a few recurring ways:
list: Tied to a trishul pendant, copying how Shiva's trident is shown in temple art.
As a standalone pendant, often with tiny beads at the waist to mimic the real drum.
As a charm on men's kadas or bracelets, especially around Shravan.
Engraved or set on rudraksha chains alongside Om or a Shiva face.
In temple-style pieces where it sits within a larger Shiva or Nataraja design.

sections.heading: How to wear a damru motif
paragraphs: Because the damru is small and rounded, it is one of the easier Shiva symbols to wear daily. It does not have the sharp outline of a trishul, so it sits comfortably under a shirt collar. On its own it looks understated; tied to a trishul it becomes more recognisably devotional.

Many people wear damru designs during Shravan, on Mondays, for Mahashivratri or while travelling on a yatra. If you like the trishul and damru together, the [rudraksha chain malas at Varaha](/divine) include Trishul and Shiva pendant designs in gold-plated metal on a bead chain. As with other sacred motifs, the usual custom is to wear it above the waist and to keep it the right way up.

sections.heading: Small details that separate a good piece
paragraphs: Look at the waist of the damru on any pendant you are considering. A well-made design shows the narrow centre clearly and keeps both ends the same size, so the shape reads correctly even from a distance. Tiny hanging beads should be firmly attached, because they are the first thing to snag on a sweater. If the damru is tied to a trishul, check that it does not spin round and hide behind the shaft. For plated pieces, keep them dry and away from perfume so the fine detail does not dull.

faq.a: Traditionally it stands for sound, rhythm and creation. It is closely linked with Shiva as Nataraja and with the origin of Sanskrit grammar in popular stories.

faq.q: Why is a damru tied to Shiva's trishul?
faq.a: Temple art often shows the two together, the trishul as Shiva's weapon and the damru as his drum, so jewellery follows that image.

faq.q: Can a damru pendant be worn daily?
faq.a: Yes. Its small rounded shape makes it comfortable for daily wear. Remove plated pieces before bathing to protect the finish.
